barriers.description: Participant sampling was biased toward computer-literate young people who already had easy access to smartphones, limiting the designers' exposure to less tech-savvy or non-smartphone users.
barriers.justification: This participation bias constrained designers' ability to manage evolving user understanding and to study the full context of use and requirements for users without smartphone access, reducing the validity of requirements and potential design adaptations for those groups.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Our user groups were diverse, even though relatively small, with participating patients having different JIA subtypes at various stages of their treatment and from different ethnical backgrounds. The app’s design and evaluation were not affected by the characteristics of YP, but participation bias may have influenced the themes that emerged from our FGDs and interviews. For example, all study participants were computer literate and had easy access to smartphones; whether further refinements of the app are necessary for patients who are less familiar with this technology needs to be established.

barriers.description: Health care professionals (HCPs) raised concerns about accessibility for all patients and the additional resources and time required to monitor and interpret patient-generated app data.
barriers.justification: These stakeholder constraints imposed limits on designers' ability to integrate the system into clinical workflows and specified requirements (eg, desktop version, data presentation), and they created resource-based barriers that affected specification of user requirements and coordination with clinical teams.
barriers.reference_excerpt: The HCPs also identified possible barriers to integration such as accessibility to all patients and demands for additional resources. For example, HCPs proposed that a desktop version of the app will be beneficial to allow access to YP without a mobile phone. In addition, HCPs were concerned about the additional time needed to monitor remote symptom deteriorations and interpret additional information collected from the app.

barriers.description: A project-level decision (driven by clinical workflow concerns) limited the study to non–real-time data monitoring, preventing designers from evaluating real-time monitoring functionality during this stage.
barriers.justification: The explicit choice not to monitor data in real time restricted the designers' ability to evaluate and iterate on features that depend on real-time monitoring, thereby hindering design evaluation and integration testing in realistic clinical use contexts.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Therefore, before downloading the app, participants will be informed that data will not be monitored in real time for this stage of the project but will be reviewed during clinic consultations. This is also explicitly explained on the app with a disclosure statement.
